headline: Nothing that runs at render time is free, and the shipped defaults now split three ways: next-yak's css-prop fold ties hand-written `vanilla` at every composition depth on 2.66 kB of payload, the build-time atomic lanes trade their zero runtime for class-attribute bytes that cost `bamboo` and `panda` more react-dom time than their styling ever cost, and the hashing libraries still pay per render, per instance, on the server and again in the browser.

findings.title: Build-time compilation moved the cost, it did not remove it
findings.prose: Every lane that resolves its classes during the build reports a library slice of roughly zero on the SSR profile, and then the ordering among them is decided by markup. On the Example `realistic-button` shown below, `stylex-layers` writes 548 B of HTML per instance with 8-character hashed class names and spends 30.5 ms in react-dom, while `bamboo` writes 1.10 kB of readable atomic names carrying 11 HTML-escaped characters per instance and its react-dom slice reaches 85.5 ms, which is the entire 2.4× SSR gap between two lanes that both do no styling work at all. The Example `tabs` shown below makes it plainer: `bamboo`'s own package costs 0.011 ms of library slice and the case still costs it 3.24 ms, because 76.6 of its 88.8 ms of JS is react-dom escaping selector text out of the class attribute. Naming is a performance decision, not a readability one.

findings.title: The css-prop fold is the only path that ignores composition depth
findings.prose: Down the composition ladder (the Examples `compose-1`, `compose-3` and `compose-6` shown below) `next-yak-css-9.7` concatenates the whole chain into one class on the plain element and renders at 0.522, 0.517 and 0.517 ms/1k on a payload of 2.67, 2.66 and 2.66 kB gzipped. Everything that merges classes instead pays per level: `bamboo` runs a `cx()` join per level and climbs 0.508 to 1.12 ms/1k, `stylex-layers` runs `styleq` and climbs 0.530 to 1.36, `panda` re-resolves each level's object and reaches 17.8. next-yak's styled API rises only from 0.448 to 0.698 ms/1k once its perf runtime collapses the `Yak → Yak` chain, against the 9.6.0 runtime's 1.17 to 5.07, but it keeps a residual wrapper wherever a styled component wraps another component, which is what costs it 1.77 against `vanilla`'s 0.838 ms/1k on the Example `tabs` shown below.

findings.title: A compiler that refuses the slow pattern beats one that falls back to it
findings.prose: `bamboo` and `panda` expose the same `css()` API, and on the Example `compose-1` shown below they ship a byte-identical source file: one `css()` object literal inside a component. `bamboo` renders it at 0.508 ms/1k because its Vite plugin replaces the call with the resulting class string; `panda` renders it at 5.14 because `css()` resolves the object on every render, 5.59 ms of component self-time. The Example `btn-variant` shown below repeats the lesson with variants, where `panda` merges conditional objects at render for 13.4 ms/1k while `bamboo`'s compiler rejects that shape outright and forces five static calls joined by `cx()`, landing at 0.647. `panda`'s own `cva` recipe reaches 0.941 from the same CSS, so the fast path exists in both libraries; the difference is whether the compiler lets you off it.

findings.title: Runtime hashing costs twice, once per render and again in the browser
findings.prose: The libraries that name a class from its content pay on the server and then repeat the work on the client. On the Example `product-grid` shown below, `@emotion/hash` and `@emotion/styled` split most of `emotion`'s 391 ms JS window and its interaction cost reaches 52.6 ms against the static-class lanes' 8.3-11.2. The browser side is worse: `goober` and `styled-components` inject their sheet during hydration, so the Example `tabs` shown below records 2.25-2.33 ms of style recalculation and a 3.5-3.9 ms layout pass inside a span where every extracted lane shows zero, and on the naive dynamic Example `dyn-translate` shown below `goober` mints a thousand distinct classes and its cold mount reaches 1320 ms against a 65.7 ms floor. Extraction is the whole cure, and it is paid for at build time instead — `panda` and `stylex-layers` cold-build in 305-434 ms and `bamboo` in 1990 ms against 72-129 ms for everything else.

findings.title: Dynamic values are a feature in next-yak and a discipline everywhere else
findings.prose: next-yak compiles a dynamic value into a static class plus a CSS custom property automatically, so its numbers are identical on the naive Example `dyn-translate` and the hand-optimized Example `dyn-fair` shown below (1.18 against 1.23 ms/1k) — there was nothing to change. Everyone else sits in one case or the other depending on developer discipline: `goober` renders at 5.98 ms/1k and mounts in 1320 ms with the naive pattern, then at 1.06 ms/1k and 86.1 ms once a person splits the static class from the inline style by hand. That split is a build-time optimization performed manually, per component, on every dynamic value, forever, and the naive case is what the same code costs when nobody pays it. `bamboo` takes the third route and refuses to compile the naive pattern at all, which is why it has no entry in `dyn-translate`.

findings.title: Payload separates the extracted lanes from everything else on a real page
findings.prose: On the Example `product-grid` shown below, a page of 400 tiles, `next-yak-css-9.7` ships 7.14 kB gzipped and hand-written `vanilla` 7.79, while atomic and utility naming roughly doubles or triples that: `stylex-layers` 13.0 kB, `bamboo` 17.2, `panda` 21.2, `cnfast` 27.7. The mechanism is that atomic systems write every rule twice, once into the sheet and once into the class attribute of every element that uses it, so payload grows with element count rather than with rule count. The Example `tabs` shown below is the extreme: the css-prop fold ships 2.37 kB against `panda`'s 15.1 for identical CSS, and the same fold holds that figure at every composition depth.

libraryHints.hint: Both APIs hold flat under composition now; the open lever is teaching the styled fold through `styled(Component)` seams, worth 1.77 → 0.86 ms/1k on `tabs`.
Zero styling runtime, but readable class names put the selector text in the markup: `tabs` spends 76.6 of 88.8 ms in react-dom escaping it. Offer hashed class names in production builds.

`css()` resolves per render wherever a call is not hoisted (`compose-1` 5.59 ms of component self-time from the same source `bamboo` compiles away); fold static call sites to their class string at build time.
Nothing on the render path for flat JSX; `styleq`'s per-element merge is the remaining cost, climbing 0.530 to 1.36 ms/1k from one composition level to six.

`generateAndInjectStyles` re-hashes and injects per render (4.23 ms of the `realistic-button` slice); hash the static rule once and ride dynamic values on a variable, as its own `.attrs` path already does.
`murmur2` re-hashes the whole serialized string every render (101 of 224 ms of JS on `realistic-button`); memoize the hash on the serialized-string identity for static components.
The compile-and-hash runs per render and injects a class per distinct value (`dyn-translate` mounts in 1320 ms); key the cache on the tagged-template identity, not the interpolated result.
The merge rebuilds and re-looks-up the joined-class key every render (1.68 ms of the `realistic-button` slice); cache on argument identity, or hoist a fully static merge to a constant.
Near-free on repeated class lists; only high-cardinality dynamic classes cost, via the cache miss. Split the invariant prefix from the volatile token so the prefix stays a hit.
